idiom_name: one entry module/class exposing use-case operations that delegate to subsystem collaborators
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: choose the few tasks clients perform and expose them as coarse operations on a single entry type, module or namespace; keep subsystem collaborators behind that entry point, inject them rather than constructing them inside, and never mirror the subsystem's method set one-for-one. Hide the subsystem's types from the public surface (packages, modules, files, access levels or opaque handles) so the entry point is the only way in, and decide explicitly whether the entry point owns the subsystem's lifecycle. The classic delegating class is only one rendering: in package-oriented languages the entry point is more often a module of functions, and in C a header plus one translation unit. Prefer returning facade-owned DTOs or result objects over raw subsystem types to avoid re-coupling callers. When coordinating independent parallel work, reason about thread-safety of subsystem objects before using concurrent execution.
code_sketch:
entry = EntryPoint(collaborator_a, collaborator_b)   # wiring injected at the edge
entry.run_use_case(request)                           # one coarse operation
# inside: validate -> call collaborators in order -> translate errors -> return facade types
# public surface: entry operations + facade-owned types only; subsystem types stay private
pitfalls: Mirroring the subsystem's method set one-to-one: the entry point must expose tasks, not internals.
Letting the entry point grow into a god object or service locator as the subsystem gains features.
Exposing subsystem types or their errors in the public signatures, which re-couples callers to the internals the facade was hiding.
Returning raw subsystem aggregates or entities instead of DTOs — callers become coupled to subsystem internal types.
Adding domain/business logic into the facade, blurring the boundary between orchestration and rule ownership.
Not handling partial failure in multi-step operations — compensating transactions or rollback must be implemented when a later step fails after an earlier one commits.
Using concurrent execution for subsystem calls without verifying thread-safety of the subsystem objects.

Wrong move: wrapping a well-designed library API one-for-one 'for safety' -> you pay indirection, stack-trace depth and maintenance cost while adding no orchestration value -> instead call the library directly and introduce a facade only when real sequencing, substitution, or vocabulary translation appears.

Wrong move: growing per-component facades in a state-management app (e.g. NgRx facades) that mix dispatches and selectors ad hoc -> the facade layer becomes an untracked second API full of one-off methods -> instead expose only use-case-level operations, keep the facade coarse, and review every added method against the client task it serves.

Wrong move: storing per-request state in a shared facade bean (the JdbcTemplate pattern is configured once and injected everywhere) -> concurrent callers corrupt each other's state -> instead keep facades stateless, pass per-call data as arguments, and verify subsystem thread-safety before sharing instances.
